items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Art Blakey came and wanted to hire him in his band but I don’t know exactly what happened but he didn’t go.

ctx.x: Did he continue to play in New Orleans some?

Yeah he played a lot with like Paul Barbarin, Uncle Lester Santiago played piano in the band, and when my dad first came back, my uncle was like, “Man you’d better learn to play some of this music.” And my dad wasn’t playing traditional music at all. So he and my uncle Lester used to practice together. They lived on Villere Street in the Tremaine. That’s where my uncle used to live. And my dad said he would go over there just about every day, they’d go over a few songs and that’s how he met my mom, practicing…

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I mean when I hear Wynton with the Art Blakey band, he was playing the living hell out of the trumpet.

ctx.x: You know? So either you’re 17, you know or 20; or you’re 94 or something like this. And these are the people that are being recorded. And these — that is not the best era of a musician’s career, when you’re very, very young — I mean when I hear Wynton with the Art Blakey band, he was playing the living hell out of the trumpet. Whew. Man, that guy was playing some really great trumpet. So there are exceptions to this rule. But most of these contracts are going to these kids. And I think that’s why people aren’t…
those beautiful things, “I Loves You Porgy” and all of those kinds. And this is what’s happening. Marketing is like you know taking the art out of art.
